//: Where the release gate gets its text. The text itself is not here and must not be:
these are third-party published works, and what this repo commits is the per-rule
counts plus a fingerprint, so a release review is a delta rather than a re-triage.
Every corpus is rebuildable. `node scripts/fetch-corpus.ts` reads the frozen URL
list under gates/sources/ and writes the documents into gates/corpora/<id>/, which
is gitignored. That is the point: a gate whose corpus cannot be rebuilt is a number
nobody else can check. It was seven of eight until the de-DE corpus stopped being a
private registry extract and became the BSI's own published XML; there is now no
corpus here that a checkout plus a network cannot reproduce, and no --consumer flag.
A corpus qualifies only if it is professionally typeset. That is the whole
subtlety of this gate and the easiest thing to get wrong: sloppy text makes
nearly every finding a true positive, which measures recall, which nobody
doubts. In text somebody set properly, every finding is a suspected false
positive by construction, and the false-positive rate is the failure mode these
rules actually have.
Corpora are chosen per rule, not per language. Three of these exist only because
one rule needed material the other corpora do not contain: aepd-faq-es is where
es.unpaired-question meets several hundred correctly opened interrogatives,
admin-ch-medien-de-ch is where the Swiss guillemet rules meet Swiss guillemets,
and theconversation-fr is where fr.space-before-high-punctuation meets question
marks, which formal academic French barely uses. Their partners cover scale and
register instead.

corpora.note: Articles from three OpenEdition journals: Revue francaise des sciences de l'information et de la communication, Questions de communication, and Terrain. Academic French set properly by the platform, which is what qualifies it: guillemets carry a real no-break space and apostrophes are U+2019, so a finding here is a suspected false positive rather than a recall test. Three journals so that one copy editor's habits do not stand in for published French.

The Conversation France. Academic authors edited by a newsroom, which is a different register from the journals: direct questions and exclamations, the interrogative punctuation formal academic prose barely contains. This is where fr.space-before-high-punctuation meets real question marks. English-language articles in the French feed were dropped by checking the extracted text, since English prose manufactures French findings the publisher never wrote.

BSI IT-Grundschutz-Kompendium, Edition 2023, from the agency's own DocBook XML. Published by a federal agency and edited to a house standard, which is what makes it usable here. No region selector: the whole document is BSI's text. This replaced a private registry extract of the same Kompendium, which held a quarter of the text and a sixth of the German quotation marks; the XML is the publisher's structured original, so the spacing and the quotation marks are exactly as BSI set them.
Ley Orgánica 3/2018, from the Boletín Oficial del Estado. Spain's official gazette, set by the state printer. Legal register: guillemets and no interrogatives at all.
The Spanish data protection agency's public FAQ. Every entry is a question, which is the only material here that puts es.unpaired-question in front of correctly opened interrogatives at any volume.
FundéuRAE articles. The foundation the Real Academia Española promotes with the Agencia EFE, whose subject is correct Spanish, so a typographic finding in its own prose is worth reading.
Swiss Federal Constitution, German, consolidated 3 March 2024, from Fedlex. Long formal Swiss German with around 700 real no-break spaces and no quotation marks whatsoever.

Press releases of the Swiss federal administration, German edition, set to the Federal Chancellery house standard. This is the corpus that carries Swiss guillemets, which the Constitution does not contain.
